analysis.one_liner: Repeals the government's authority to wind down failing big financial firms and replaces it with a special bankruptcy process.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2013 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day, the bill never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal Title II of the Dodd-Frank law, which gives regulators power to seize and dismantle a failing giant financial company outside of bankruptcy court. In its place it would create a new 'Chapter 14' of the bankruptcy code with special rules and judges for big financial companies, and it would bar the Federal Reserve from lending money to keep such companies alive during their bankruptcy. Supporters, all Republicans, framed it as ending bank bailouts and saving taxpayer money; critics warned that bankruptcy alone may not be able to safely dismantle a failing giant bank in a crisis.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, large financial companies — bank holding companies and firms mostly engaged in financial activities — would escape the Dodd-Frank receivership regime and instead go through a bankruptcy process with specialized judges, sealed emergency hearings, and rules allowing parts of the business to move to a new 'bridge' company. Proponents argued taxpayers would benefit because the Federal Reserve could no longer lend to prop up a failing firm. In practice, the companies themselves gained the most: more freedom in how their failures were handled and the end of a resolution process they disliked.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Title II of Dodd-Frank (Orderly Liquidation Authority), the law allowing regulators to liquidate a failing large financial company outside normal bankruptcy.
Creates a new Chapter 14 in bankruptcy law for 'covered financial corporations,' with a special trustee, a bridge company mechanism, transfers of assets, and exemption from certain securities laws.
Requires the Chief Justice to designate expert district and bankruptcy judges to handle these cases, with emergency hearings held within 12 hours and transcripts sealed until the case ends.
Prohibits Federal Reserve banks from making advances for debtor-in-possession financing to a covered financial corporation in Chapter 14 or to its bridge company.

analysis.who_pays: The main cost is risk-shifting in a crisis. If a giant financial firm failed under ordinary court bankruptcy instead of an orderly receivership, the disruption would land on the broader economy — savers, workers, borrowers, and businesses that depend on functioning credit markets. Creditors and derivatives counterparties would also face new rules on when they can terminate contracts and what claims they can pursue.
analysis.who_pays_short: The broader economy in a crisis

drawbacks.text: The central objection: a specialized bankruptcy process may not be able to dismantle a failing systemically important firm quickly or safely enough to prevent the kind of market panic that followed Lehman Brothers' collapse in 2008, when there was no resolution authority in place.

The bill repeals a resolution regime that was funded by assessments on large financial companies rather than general taxpayers, so the 'taxpayer savings' claim is contested — the money at risk in a crisis would come from the wider economy either way.

Emergency hearings under the bill occur within 12 hours, with notice limited to the firm, the FDIC, and Treasury, and transcripts sealed until the case ends — a process critics could call both too rushed and too opaque for a decision affecting the entire financial system.

The bill gives the Federal Reserve discretion to file the bankruptcy petition and certify financial instability, replacing one form of discretionary government intervention with another rather than removing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — that failing giant financial firms should go through bankruptcy rather than a regulator-run liquidation — is a serious policy argument, and the ban on Federal Reserve lending to bankrupt firms is a real constraint on backdoor bailouts. But the trade is unbalanced: it strips away a tested, industry-funded orderly liquidation framework in favor of an untested bankruptcy process whose workability in an actual crisis was heavily disputed. The benefits accrue mainly to the firms escaping the regime; the downside risk of a botched windup in a panic would be borne by everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a vote, or floor time before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Cornyn introduced S. 1861 on December 19, 2013, naming Sen. Pat Toomey as an original co-sponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The bill would repeal Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act (Orderly Liquidation Authority) and add a new Chapter 14 to federal bankruptcy law for covered financial corporations.
The full action history shows no further action — no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the Dodd-Frank orderly liquidation authority remained in place and large financial companies stayed subject to the receivership regime they sought to escape. No taxpayer or industry money changed hands; the status quo the bill targeted was preserved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Dodd-Frank resolution regime and its backers

for.name: Sen. Pat Toomey
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original co-sponsor.

against.what_they_did: Publicly argued that bankruptcy alone could not handle the failure of a systemically important financial firm and opposed repealing the orderly liquidation authority.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded; the bill died in a Senate committee controlled by Democrats without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies and systemically important financial firms
industries.note: The bill frees these firms from Dodd-Frank's orderly liquidation authority and the FDIC receivership process, replacing it with a bankruptcy route they generally preferred. The ban on Federal Reserve lending to a firm in bankruptcy removes some emergency support, but the headline effect is escape from a regime designed to wind them down without a panic.

The bill repeals the FDIC's authority to act as receiver for failing large financial companies under Dodd-Frank Title II, leaving it only a limited role in bankruptcy transfers. Losing that authority reduces the government's tool for preventing a chaotic collapse that would hit ordinary depositors and borrowers.
